title: Infrastructure Australia Bill 2008
portfolio: Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development and Local Government

divisions.question: That the amendments ( **Mr Truss’s** ) be agreed to.

speeches.speaker: Penny Wong
speeches.brief: The Rudd Labor Government moved to establish Infrastructure Australia as a statutory advisory council to develop a national infrastructure blueprint, conduct a National Infrastructure Audit and produce a priority list within 12 months, citing an estimated $6.4 billion annual loss from underinvestment and $9.4 billion in 2005 urban congestion costs.

speeches.speaker: Nigel Scullion
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the previous coalition government had already established national infrastructure planning through AusLink (with $15.8 billion in funding for 2004‑05 to 2008‑09 and $22.3 billion for 2009‑2013‑14) and COAG, making Infrastructure Australia a potentially redundant bureaucracy, and criticised Labor for cutting $65 million in rail maintenance and breaking a $780 million promise on the F3 to Braxton link road. The speaker also announced the coalition would move amendments to require parliamentary scrutiny of ministerial directions and to allow Infrastructure Australia to independently review projects.

speeches.speaker: Christine Milne
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the definition of nationally significant infrastructure in the Infrastructure Australia Bill 2008 should be expanded to explicitly include social infrastructure such as schools, universities, hospitals and libraries, and also raised concerns that the Bill did not mandate consideration of infrastructure needs in Indigenous communities.
The committee resumed consideration of the Infrastructure Australia Bill 2008 and the Greens amendment (5) moved by Senator Milne, with the question being whether the amendment should be agreed to.

speeches.speaker: Christine Milne
speeches.brief: An amendment was argued to require that infrastructure projects over $50 million recommended by Infrastructure Australia be referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Public Works for scrutiny. The government opposed the amendment, stating it was unnecessary and that existing parliamentary processes already provide accountability.

The House of Representatives disagreed to Senate amendments to the Infrastructure Australia Bill 2008 and requested reconsideration; the Senate ordered immediate consideration of the message in Committee of the Whole.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Conroy
speeches.brief: The opposition moved not to insist on its amendments to the Infrastructure Australia bill, expressing disappointment that the government rejected amendments aimed at transparency, independence, and scrutiny of election promises. Other parties also declined to insist, with the Greens criticising the bill for making greenhouse gas advice discretionary rather than mandatory.
